content.title: Area Between Curves
content.overview: Calculating the area of a region bounded by two or more curves involves identifying the boundaries of the region and integrating the difference between the upper and lower functions (or right and left functions) over the specified interval.
learning_objectives: Identify intersection points of two functions to determine integration limits.
Determine which function is the 'top' or 'bottom' on a given interval.
Set up and evaluate definite integrals to find the area between curves with respect to x or y.
Handle regions where the relative positions of the curves change by splitting the integral.

sections.title: The Intersect-Top-Integrate Strategy
sections.content:
To find the area between two curves, y = f(x) and y = g(x), follow three main steps. First, find the intersection points by setting f(x) = g(x); these values typically serve as your limits of integration (a and b). Second, determine which function is greater on the interval [a, b]. You can do this by testing a value within the interval or analyzing the graphs. Third, set up the integral of the 'top' function minus the 'bottom' function: Area = ∫[f(x) - g(x)] dx. If the curves intersect multiple times such that the top function changes, you must split the area into separate integrals for each subinterval and sum their absolute values.

![A flow chart showing the steps: 1. Find Intersections, 2. Identify Top/Bottom, 3. Set up Integral, 4. Evaluate and Sum.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/b6810073-4efd-4d69-b485-6c85e83518b4-1786519386148-867.webp)

sections.title: Integrating with Respect to y
sections.content: Sometimes it is more efficient to integrate with respect to y, especially if the boundaries are given as x = f(y) and x = g(y). In this case, the limits of integration are the y-coordinates of the intersection points. The integrand is defined as the 'right' function minus the 'left' function: Area = ∫[x_right - x_left] dy. This approach is necessary when a single vertical line would intersect a curve more than once, making it difficult to define a single 'top' or 'bottom' function in terms of x.

worked_examples.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabola y = x^2 + 2x + 3 and the line y = 2x + 5.
worked_examples.solution:
1. Find intersections: Set x^2 + 2x + 3 = 2x + 5. This simplifies to x^2 = 2, so x = -√2 and x = √2.
2. Determine the top function: Test x = 0. For the parabola, y(0) = 3. For the line, y(0) = 5. Since 5 > 3, the line y = 2x + 5 is the top function on the interval [-√2, √2].
3. Set up the integral: Area = ∫ from -√2 to √2 [(2x + 5) - (x^2 + 2x + 3)] dx = ∫ from -√2 to √2 (-x^2 + 2) dx.
4. Evaluate: [-x^3/3 + 2x] from -√2 to √2. 
At √2: -(2√2)/3 + 2√2 = 4√2/3. 
At -√2: -(-2√2)/3 - 2√2 = -4√2/3. 
Subtracting: (4√2/3) - (-4√2/3) = 8√2/3 square units.

common_mistakes: Integrating 'bottom minus top', which results in a negative area value.
Failing to split the integral when the curves cross each other within the interval of integration.
Using x-limits for an integral set up with respect to dy, or vice versa.
Confusing the area between curves with the area under a single curve (forgetting to subtract the second function).
exam_tips: Always sketch the region or use a test point to verify which function is on top.
Area must always be a non-negative value; if you get a negative result, check your subtraction order.
If a calculator is permitted, use the absolute value of the difference, ∫|f(x) - g(x)| dx, to automatically handle crossing curves.
Check if the problem provides specific units (e.g., meters) and ensure the final answer is in square units.
content.recap: To find the area between curves, identify the intersection points for bounds, determine the relative vertical or horizontal positions of the functions, and integrate the difference (Top - Bottom for dx; Right - Left for dy).

knowledge_claims.content: To find the limits of integration for the area between two curves, set the two functions equal to each other and solve for the variable of integration.
The integrand for the area between two curves with respect to x is defined as the upper function minus the lower function.
The integrand for the area between two curves with respect to y is defined as the rightmost function minus the leftmost function.
The calculated area between two curves must always be a non-negative value.
If two curves intersect at more than two points within the interval of interest, the area must be calculated by splitting the integral at each intersection point.
Integrating with respect to y is often preferred when the boundary functions are expressed as x in terms of y or when the region is bounded by left and right curves.
A common error is using the x-coordinates of intersection points as limits when integrating with respect to y.
The general formula for the area between f(x) and g(x) from a to b is the integral from a to b of the absolute value of the difference, |f(x) - g(x)|.
The area between curves represents the total accumulated difference between two rates or quantities over a specific interval.
When curves are given in terms of x, testing a single x-value between intersections determines which function is 'top' for that entire subinterval.
Unlike the area under a single curve, which can be negative if the curve is below the x-axis, the area between two curves is strictly the magnitude of the region between them.
If the result of a 'top minus bottom' integral is negative, it indicates the functions were likely assigned to the wrong positions in the integrand.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Area Between Curves — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Area Between Curves: Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes.
options.B: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.
options.C: Ratio and Root Tests: Ratio and root limits below one imply absolute convergence and above one imply divergence, while a limit of one is inconclusive.
options.D: Derivative as a Limit: The derivative is the limit of average rates of change and represents instantaneous rate of change or tangent-line slope.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Area Between Curves — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Polar Area: Polar area over an angular interval is one half the integral of the squared radius, with intersections determining correct angular bounds.
options.B: Area Between Curves: Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes.
options.C: Taylor and Maclaurin Series: Taylor coefficients are derivatives evaluated at the center divided by factorials, and Maclaurin series are centered at zero.
options.D: Differentiability and Continuity: Differentiability implies continuity, but corners, cusps, vertical tangents, discontinuities, and unequal one-sided derivatives can prevent differentiability.

items.explanation: Choice B is best because Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.
